speeches.speaker: VOICE ON THE RADIO
speeches.text: ...and according to Scotland Yard, the crime took place at twenty-four Culver Street, Paddington. The murdered woman was a Mrs. Maureen Lyon. In connection with the murder, the police are anxious to interview a man seen in the vicinity, wearing a dark overcoat, light scarf, and a soft felt hat. Motorists are warned against ice-bound roads. The heavy snow is expected to continue, and throughout the country there will be a certain freezing, particularly at points on the north and northeast coast of Scotland.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Mrs. Barlow! Mrs. Barlow! Brr! It's cold. It really does look nice ― oh! How stupid of Giles. Gosh!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie? Mollie? Mollie? Where are you?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Doing all the work, you brute.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh, there you are ― leave it all to me. Shall I stoke the Aga?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Done.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Hullo, sweetheart. Your nose is cold.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I've just come in.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Why? Where have you been? Surely you've not been out in this weather?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I had to go down to the village for some stuff I'd forgotten. Did you get the chicken netting?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It wasn't the right kind. I went on to another dump but that wasn't any good either. Practically a whole day wasted. My God, I'm half frozen. Car was skidding like anything. The snow's coming down thick. What do you bet we're not snowed up tomorrow?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh dear, I do hope not. If only the pipes don't freeze.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: We'll have to keep the central heating well-stoked up. H'm, not too good ― I wish they'd send the coke along. We've not got any too much.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh! I do so want everything to go well at first. First impressions are so important.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Is everything ready? Nobody's arrived yet, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, thank goodness. I think everything's in order. Mrs. Barlow's hooked it early. Afraid of the weather, I suppose.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What a nuisance these daily women are. That leaves everything on your shoulders.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And yours! This is a partnership.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: So long as you don't ask me to cook.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, no, that's my department. Anyway, we've got lots of tins in case we are snowed up. Oh, Giles, do you think it's going to be all right?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Got cold feet, have you? Are you sorry now we didn't sell the place when your aunt left it to you, instead of having this mad idea of running it as a guest house?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, I'm not. I love it. And talking of a guest house. Just look at that!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Pretty good, what?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's a disaster! Don't you see? You've left out the "S". Monkwell instead of Monkswell.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Good Lord, so I did. However did I come to do that? But it doesn't really matter, does it? Monkwell is as good a name.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You're in disgrace. Go and stoke up the central heating.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Across that icy yard! Ugh! Shall I bank it up for the night now?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, you don't do that until ten or eleven o'clock at night.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: How appalling!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Hurry up. Someone may arrive at any minute now.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You've got all the rooms worked out?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes. Mrs. Boyle, Front Fourposter Room. Major Metcalf, Blue Room. Miss Casewell, East Room. Mr. Wren, Oak Room.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I wonder what all these people will be like. Oughtn't we to have got rent in advance?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh no, I don't think so.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: We're rather mugs at this game.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They bring luggage. If they don't pay we hang on to their luggage. It's quite simple.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I can't help thinking we ought to have taken a correspondence course in hotel keeping. We're sure to get had in some way. Their luggage might be just bricks wrapped up in newspaper, and where should we be then?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They all wrote from very good addresses.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: That's what servants with forged references do. Some of these people may be criminals hiding from the police.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't care what they are so long as they pay us seven guineas every week.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You're such a wonderful woman of business, Mollie.

speeches.speaker: VOICE ON THE RADIO
speeches.text: And according to Scotland Yard, the crime took place at twenty-four Culver Street, Paddington. The murdered woman was a Mrs. Maureen Lyon. In connection with the murder, the police ― ― are anxious to interview a man seen in the vicinity, wearing a dark overcoat ― ― light scarf ― ― and a soft felt hat. Motorists are warned against icebound roads. The heavy snow is expected to continue, and throughout the country...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: How do you do?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Thanks so much. Weather is simply awful. My taxi gave up at your gate. Wouldn't attempt the drive. No sporting instinct. Are you Mrs. Ralston? How delightful! My name's Wren.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: How do you do, Mr. Wren?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: You know you're not at all as I'd pictured you. I've been thinking of you as a retired General's widow, Indian Army. I thought you'd be terrifically grim and Memsahibish, and that the whole place would be simply crammed with Benares brass. Instead, it's heavenly. ― quite heavenly. Lovely proportions. That's a fake! Ah, but this table's genuine. I'm simply going to love this place. Have you got any wax flowers or birds of Paradise?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'm afraid not.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What a pity! Well, what about a sideboard? A purple plummy mahogany sideboard with great solid carved fruits on it?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, we have ― in the dining room.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: In here? I must see it.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Do come and warm yourself.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Absolutely perfect. Real bedrock respectability. But why do away with a centre mahogany table? Little tables just spoil the effect.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We thought guests would prefer them ― this is my husband.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: How do you do? Terrible weather, isn't it? Takes one back to Dickens and Scrooge and that irritating Tiny Tim. So bogus. Of course, Mrs. Ralston, you're absolutely right about the little tables. I was being carried away by my feeling for period. If you had a mahogany dining table, you'd have to have the right family round it. Stern handsome father with a beard, prolific, faded mother, eleven children of assorted ages, a grim governess, and somebody called "poor Harriet," the poor relation who acts as general dogsbody and is very, very grateful for being given a good home!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll take your suitcase upstairs for you. Oak Room, did you say?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I do hope that it's got a fourposter with little chintz roses?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It hasn't.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I don't believe your husband is going to like me. How long have you been married? Are you very much in love?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We've been married just a year. Perhaps you'd like to go up and see your room?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Ticked off! But I do so like knowing all about people. I mean, I think people are so madly interesting. Don't you?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, I suppose some are and some are not.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No, I don't agree. They're all interesting, because you never really know what anyone is like ― or what they are really thinking. For instance, you don't know what I'm thinking about now, do you?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Not in the least. Cigarette?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No, thank you. You see? The only people who really know what other people are like are artists ― and they don't know why they know it! But if they're portrait painters it comes out ― on the canvas.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Are you a painter?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No, I'm an architect. My parents, you know, baptized me Christopher, in the hope that I would be an architect. Christopher Wren! As good as halfway home. Actually, of course, everyone laughs about it and makes jokes about St. Paul's. However ― who knows?― I may yet have the last laugh. Chris Wren's Prefab Nests may yet go down in history! I'm going to like it here. I find your wife most sympathetic.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Indeed.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: And really very beautiful.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, don't be absurd.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: There, isn't that like an Englishwoman? Compliments always embarrass them. European women take compliments as a matter of course, but Englishwomen have all the feminine spirit crushed out of them by their husbands. There's something very boorish about English husbands.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Come up and see your room.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Shall I?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Could you stoke up the hot-water boiler?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: This is Monkswell Manor, I presume?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Yes...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I am Mrs. Boyle.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'm Giles Ralston. Come in to the fire, Mrs. Boyle, and get warm. Awful weather, isn't it? Is this your only luggage?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: A Major ― Metcalf, is it?― is seeing to it.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll leave the door for him.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: The taxi wouldn't risk coming up the drive. It stopped at the gate. We had to share a taxi from the station ― and there was great difficulty in getting that. Nothing ordered to meet us, it seems.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'm so sorry. We didn't know what train you would be coming by, you see, otherwise, of course, we'd have seen that someone was ― er ― standing by.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: All trains should have been met.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Let me take your coat. My wife will be here in a moment. I'll just go along and give Metcalf a hand with the bags.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: The drive might at least have been cleared of snow. Most offhand and casual, I must say.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'm so sorry I...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes. I...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: You're very young.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Young?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: To be running an establishment of this kind. You can't have had much experience.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: There has to be a beginning for everything, hasn't there?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I see. Quite inexperienced. An old, old house. I hope you haven't got dry rot.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Certainly not!

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: A lot of people don't know they have got dry rot until it's too late to do anything about it.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: The house is in perfect condition.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: H'm ― it could do with a coat of paint. You know, you've got worm in this oak.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: This way, Major. This is my wife.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: How d'you do? Absolute blizzard outside. Thought at one time we shouldn't make it. Oh, I beg your pardon. If it goes on like this I should say you'll have five or six feet of snow by morning. Not seen anything like it since I was on leave in nineteen-forty.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll take these up. Which rooms did you say? Blue Room and the Rose Room.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No ― I put Mr. Wren in the Rose Room. He liked the fourposter so much. So it's Mrs. Boyle in the Oak Room and Major Metcalf in the Blue Room.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Major?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Sir!

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Do you have much servant difficulty here?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We have quite a good local woman who comes in from the village.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: And what indoor staff?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No indoor staff. Just us.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: In-deed. I understood this was a guest house in full running order.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We're only just starting.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I would have said that a proper staff of servants was essential before opening this kind of establishment. I consider your advertisement was most misleading. May I ask if I am the only guest ― with Major Metcalf, that is?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh no, there are several here.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: This weather, too. A blizzard ― no less ― all very unfortunate.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But we couldn't very well foresee the weather!

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: "The North Wind doth blow And it will bring snow And what will the robin do then, poor thing?" I adore nursery rhymes, don't you? Always so tragic and macabre. That's why children like them.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: May I introduce. Mr. Wren ― Mrs. Boyle.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: How d'you do?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: This is a very beautiful house. Don't you think so?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I have come to the time of life when the amenities of an establishment are more important than its appearance. If I had not believed this was a running concern I should never have come here. I understand it was fully equipped with every home comfort.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: There is no obligation for you to remain here if you are not satisfied, Mrs. Boyle.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: No, indeed, I should not think of doing so.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: If there has been any misapprehension it would perhaps be better if you went elsewhere. I could ring up for the taxi to return. The roads are not yet blocked. We have had so many applications for rooms that we shall be able to fill your place quite easily. In any case we are raising our terms next month.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I am certainly not going to leave before I have tried what the place is like. You needn't think you can turn me out now. Perhaps you will take me up to my bedroom, Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Certainly, Mrs. Boyle. Darling, you were wonderful...

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I think that's a perfectly horrible woman. I don't like her at all. I'd love to see you turn her out into the snow. Serve her right.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It's a pleasure I've got to forgo, I'm afraid. Lord, there's another of them. Come in ― come in.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Afraid my car's bogged about half a mile down the road ― ran into a drift.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Let me take this. Any more stuff in the car?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No, I travel light. Ha, glad to see you've got a good fire.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Er ― Mr. Wren ― Miss ―?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Casewell.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: My wife will be down in a minute.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No hurry. Got to get myself thawed out. Looks as though you're going to be snowed up here. Weather forecast says heavy falls expected. Motorists warned, etcetera. Hope you've got plenty of provisions in.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh yes. My wife's an excellent manager. Anyway, we can always eat our hens.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Before we start eating each other, eh?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Any news in the paper apart from the weather?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Usual political crisis. Oh yes, and a rather juicy murder!

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: A murder? Oh, I like murder!

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: They seem to think it was a homicidal maniac. Strangled a woman somewhere near Paddington. Sex maniac, I suppose.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Doesn't say much, does it? "The police are anxious to interview a man seen in the vicinity of Culver Street at the time. Medium height, wearing darkish overcoat, lightish scarf and soft felt hat. Police messages to this effect have been broadcast throughout the day."

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Useful description. Fit pretty well anyone, wouldn't it?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: When it says that the police are anxious to interview someone, is that a polite way of hinting that he's the murderer?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Could be.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Who was the woman who was murdered?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Mrs. Lyon. Mrs. Maureen Lyon.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Young or old?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: It doesn't say. It doesn't seem to have been robbery...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I told you ― sex maniac.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Here's Miss Casewell, Mollie. My wife.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: How d'you do?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's an awful night. Would you like to come up to your room? The water's hot if you'd like a bath.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You're right, I would.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I must hurry out to the kitchen and get on with things. Major Metcalf is very nice. He won't be difficult. It's Mrs. Boyle really frightens me. We must have a nice dinner. I was thinking of opening two tins of minced beef and cereal and a tin of peas, and mashing the potatoes. And there's stewed figs and custard. Do you think that will be all right?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh ― I should think so. Not-not very original, perhaps.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Do let me help. I adore cooking. Why not an omelette? You've got eggs, haven't you?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh yes, we've got plenty of eggs. We keep lots of fowls. They don't lay as well as they should, but we've put down a lot of eggs.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: And if you've got a bottle of cheap, any-type wine, you could add it to the ―"minced beef and cereals," did you say? Give it a continental flavour. Show me where the kitchen is and what you've got, and I daresay I shall have an inspiration.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Come on. Isn't he sweet? He's put on an apron and he's getting all the things together. He says leave it all to him and don't come back for half an hour. If our guests want to do the cooking themselves, it will save a lot of trouble.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Why on earth did you give him the best room?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I told you, he liked the fourposter.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: He liked the pretty fourposter. Twerp!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I've got no use for that kind. You didn't handle his suitcase, I did.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Had it got bricks in it?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It was no weight at all. If you ask me there was nothing inside it. He's probably one of those young men who go about bilking hotel keepers.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't believe it. I like him. I think Miss Casewell's rather peculiar, don't you?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Terrible female ― if she is a female.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It seems very hard that all our guests should be either unpleasant or odd. Anyway, I think Major Metcalf's all right, don't you?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Probably drinks!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, do you think so?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No, I don't. I was just feeling rather depressed. Well, at any rate we know the worst now. They've all arrived.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Who can that be?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Probably the Culver Street murderer.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Don't!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: A thousand pardons. I am ― where am I?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: This is Monkswell Manor Guest House.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: But what stupendous good fortune! Madame! What an answer to prayer. A guest house ― and a charming hostess. My Rolls-Royce, alas, has run into a snowdrift. Blinding snow everywhere. I do not know where I am. Perhaps, I think to myself, I shall freeze to death. And then I take a little bag, I stagger through the snow, I see before me big iron gates. A habitation! I am saved. Twice I fall into the snow as I come up your drive, but at last I arrive and immediately ― despair turns to joy. you can let me have a room ― yes?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh yes...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's rather a small one, I'm afraid.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Naturally ― naturally ― you have other guests.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We've only just opened this place as a guest house today, and so we're ― we're rather new at it.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Charming ― charming...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What about your luggage?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: That is of no consequence. I have locked the car securely.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But wouldn't it be better to get it in?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: No, no. I can assure you on such a night as this, there will be no thieves abroad. And for me, my wants are very simple. I have all I need ― here ― in this little bag. Yes, all that I need.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You'd better get thoroughly warm. I'll see about your room. I'm afraid it's rather a cold room because it faces north, but all the others are occupied.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: You have several guests, then?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: There's Mrs. Boyle and Major Metcalf and Miss Casewell and a young man called Christopher Wren ― and now ― you.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Yes ― the unexpected guest. The guest that you did not invite. The guest who just arrived ― from nowhere ― out of the storm. It sounds quite dramatic, does it not? Who am I? You do not know. Where do I come from? You do not know. Me, I am the man of mystery. But now, I tell you this. I complete the picture. From now on there will be no more arrivals. And no departures either. By tomorrow ― perhaps even already ― we are cut off from civilization. No butcher, no baker, no milkman, no postman, no daily papers ― nobody and nothing but ourselves. That is admirable ― admirable. It could not suit me better. My name, by the way, is Paravicini. Mr. and Mrs. Ralston? And this ― is Monkswell Manor Guest House, you said? Good. Monkswell Manor Guest House. Perfect. Perfect.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I consider it most dishonest not to have told me they were only just starting this place.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Well, everything's got to have a beginning, you know. Excellent breakfast this morning. Good coffee. Scrambled eggs, homemade marmalade. And all nicely served, too. Little woman does it all herself.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Amateurs ― there should be a proper staff.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Excellent lunch, too.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Cornbeef.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: But very well-disguised cornbeef. Red wine in it. Mrs. Ralston promised to make a pie for us tonight.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: These radiators are not really hot. I shall speak about it.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Very comfortable beds, too. At least mine was. Hope yours was, too.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: It was quite adequate. I don't quite see why the best bedroom should have been given to that very peculiar young man.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Got here ahead of us. First come, first served.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: From the advertisement I got quite a different impression of what this place would be like. A comfortable writing room, and a much larger place altogether ― with bridge and other amenities.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Regular old tabbies' delight.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I beg your pardon.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Er ― I mean, yes, I quite see what you mean.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: No, indeed, I shan't stay here long.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No. No, I don't suppose you will.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Really that is a very peculiar young man. Unbalanced mentally, I shouldn't wonder.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Think he's escaped from a lunatic asylum?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I shouldn't be at all surprised.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Yes?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Can you shovel the snow away again from the back door?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Coming.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I'll give you a hand, what? Good exercise. Must have exercise.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Sorry!

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: That's all right.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Really! What an incredible young woman. Doesn't she know anything about housework? Carrying a carpet sweeper through the front hall. Aren't there any back stairs?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Oh yes ― nice stairs. Very convenient if there was a fire.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Then why not use them? Anyway, all the housework should have been done in the morning before lunch.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I gather our hostess had to cook the lunch.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: All very haphazard and amateurish. There should be a proper staff.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Not very easy to get nowadays, is it?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: No, indeed, the lower classes seem to have no idea of their responsibilities.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Poor old lower classes. Got the bit between their teeth, haven't they?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I gather you are a Socialist.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Oh, I wouldn't say that. I'm not a Red ― just pale pink. But I don't take much interest in politics ― I live abroad.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I suppose conditions are much easier abroad.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I don't have to cook and clean ― as I gather most people have to do in this country.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: This country has gone sadly downhill. Not what it used to be. I sold my house last year. Everything was too difficult.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Hotels and guest houses are easier.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: They certainly solve some of one's problems. Are you over in England for long?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Depends. I've got some business to see to. When it's done ― I shall go back.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: To France?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Italy?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Would you mind not having that on quite so loud! I always find the radio rather distracting when one is trying to write letters.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Do you?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: If you don't particularly want to listen just now...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It's my favourite music. There's a writing table in there.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I know. But it's much warmer here.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Much warmer, I agree. Bloody old bitch.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Oh!

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Hullo.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Wherever I go that woman seems to hunt me down ― and then she glares at me ― positively glares.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Turn it down a bit.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Is that all right?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Oh yes, it's served its purpose.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What purpose?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Tactics, boy.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Oh, you mean her.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: She'd pinched the best chair. I've got it now.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: You drove her out. I'm glad. I'm very glad. I don't like her a bit. Let's think of things we can do to annoy her, shall we? I wish she'd go away from here.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: In this? Not a hope.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But when the snow melts.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Oh, when the snow melts lots of things may have happened.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes ― yes ― that's true. Snow's rather lovely, isn't it? So peaceful ― and pure... It makes one forget things.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It doesn't make me forget.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: How fierce you sound.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I was thinking.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What sort of thinking?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Ice on a bedroom jug, chilblains, raw and bleeding ― one thin ragged blanket ― a child shivering with cold and fear.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: My dear, it sounds too, too grim ― what is it? A novel?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You didn't know I was a writer, did you?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Are you?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Sorry to disappoint you. Actually I'm not.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes? Yes ― this is Monkswell Manor Guest House...What?...No, I'm afraid Mr. Ralston can't come to the telephone just now. This is Mrs. Ralston speaking. Who...? The Berkshire Police...? Oh yes, yes, Superintendent Hogben, I'm afraid that's impossible. He'd never get here. We're snowed up. Completely snowed up. The roads are impassable... Nothing can get through...Yes...Very well...But what... Hullo-hullo...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie, do you know where there's another spade?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles, the police have just rung up.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Trouble with police, eh? Serving liquor without a licence?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They're sending out an inspector or a sergeant or something.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But he'll never get here.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That's what I told them. But they seemed quite confident that he would.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Nonsense. Even a jeep couldn't get through today. Anyway, what's it all about?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That's what I asked. But he wouldn't say. Just said I was to impress on my husband to listen very carefully to what Sergeant Trotter, I think it was, had to say, and to follow his instructions implicitly. Isn't it extraordinary?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What on earth do you think we've done?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Do you think it's those nylons from Gibraltar?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I did remember to get the wireless licence, didn't I?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, it's in the kitchen dresser.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I had rather a near shave with the car the other day but it was entirely the other fellow's fault.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We must have done something...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Probably something to do with running this place. I expect we've ignored some tinpot regulation of some Ministry or other. You practically can't avoid it, nowadays.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh dear, I wish we'd never started this place. We're going to be snowed up for days, and everyone is cross, and we shall go through all our reserve of tins.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Cheer up, darling, everything's going all right at the moment. I've filled up all the coalscuttles, and brought in the wood, and stoked the Aga and done the hens. I'll go and do the boiler next, and chop some kindling... You know, Mollie, come to think of it, it must be something pretty serious to send a police sergeant trekking out in all this. It must be something really urgent...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Ah, there you are, Mr. Ralston. Do you know the central heating in the library is practically stone cold?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Sorry, Mrs. Boyle, we're a bit short of coke and...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I am paying seven guineas a week here ― seven guineas ― and I do not want to freeze.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll go and stoke it up.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston, if you don't mind my saying so, that is a very extraordinary young man you have staying here. His manners ― and his ties ― and does he ever brush his hair?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He's an extremely brilliant young architect.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I beg your pardon?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Christopher Wren is an architect...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: My dear young woman. I have naturally heard of Sir Christopher Wren. Of course, he was an architect. He built St. Paul's. You young people seem to think that no one is educated but yourselves.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I meant this Wren. His name is Christopher. His parents called him that because they hoped he'd be an architect. And he is ― or nearly one ― so it turned out all right.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Humph. Sounds a fishy story to me. I should make some enquiries about him if I were you. What do you know of him?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Just as much as I know about you, Mrs. Boyle ― which is that you are both paying us seven guineas a week. That is really all I need to know, isn't it? And all that concerns me. It doesn't matter to me whether I like my guests, or whether I don't.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: You are young and inexperienced and should welcome advice from someone more knowledgeable than yourself. And what about this foreigner?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What about him?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: You weren't expecting him, were you?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: To turn away a bona fide traveller is against the law, Mrs. Boyle. You should know that.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Why do you say that?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Weren't you a magistrate, sitting on the Bench, Mrs. Boyle?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: All I say is that this Paravicini, or whatever he calls himself, seems to me...

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Beware, dear lady. You talk of the devil and there he is. Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I didn't hear you come in.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I came in on tiptoe ― like this. Nobody ever hears me if I do not want them to. I find that very amusing.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Now there was a young lady...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Well, I must get on with my letters. I'll see if it's a little warmer in the drawing room.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: My charming hostess looks upset. What is it, dear lady?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Everything's rather difficult this morning. Because of the snow.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Yes. Snow makes things difficult, does it not? Or else it makes them easy. Yes ― very easy.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know what you mean.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: No, there is quite a lot you do not know. I think, for one thing, that you do not know very much about running a guest house.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I daresay we don't. But we mean to make a go of it.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Bravo ― bravo!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'm not such a very bad cook...

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: You are without doubt an enchanting cook. May I give you a little word of warning, Mrs. Ralston? You and your husband must not be too trusting, you know. Have you references with these guests of yours?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Is that usual? I always thought people just ― just came.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: It is advisable to know a little about the people who sleep under your roof. Take, for example, myself. I turn up saying that my car is overturned in a snowdrift. What do you know of me? Nothing at all! I may be a thief, a robber, a fugitive from justice ― a madman ― even ― a murderer.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh!

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: You see! And perhaps you know just as little of your other guests.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, as far as Mrs. Boyle goes...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: The drawing room is far too cold to sit in. I shall write my letters in here.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Allow me to poke the fire for you.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston, is your husband about? I'm afraid the pipes of the ― er ― the downstairs cloakroom are frozen.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh dear. What an awful day. First the police and then the pipes.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Police?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Police, did you say?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They rang up. Just now. To say they're sending a sergeant out here. But I don't think he'll ever get here.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: The ruddy coke's more than half stones. And the price... Hullo, is anything the matter?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I hear the police are on their way here. Why?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh, that's all right. No one can get through in this. Why, the drifts must be five feet deep. The roads are all banked up. Nobody will get here today. Excuse me, Mr. Paravicini. May I put these down.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Are you Mr. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Thank you, sir. Detective Sergeant Trotter. Berkshire Police. Can I get these skis off and stow them somewhere?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Go round that way to the front door. I'll meet you.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Thank you, sir.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I suppose that's what we pay our police force for, nowadays, to go round enjoying themselves at winter sports.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Why did you send for the police, Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But I didn't.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Who's that man? Where did he come from? He passed the drawing room window on skis. All over snow and looking terribly hearty.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: You may believe it or not, but the man is a policeman. A policeman ― skiing!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Er ― this is Detective Sergeant Trotter.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Good afternoon.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: You can't be a sergeant. You're too young.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm not quite as young as I look, madam.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But terribly hearty.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: We'll stow your skis away under the stairs.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Ralston, but may I use your telephone?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Of course, Major Metcalf.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: He's very attractive, don't you think so? I always think that policemen are very attractive.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: No brains. You can see that at a glance.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Hullo! Hullo!... Mrs. Ralston, this telephone is dead ― quite dead.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It was all right about half an hour ago.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: The line's gone with the weight of the snow, I suppose.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: So we're quite cut off now. Quite cut off. That's funny, isn't it?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I don't see anything to laugh at.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: No, indeed.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Ah, it's a private joke of my own. Hist, the sleuth is returning.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Now we can get to business, Mr. Ralston. Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Do you want to see us alone? If so, we can go into the library.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It's not necessary, sir. It'll save time if everybody's present. If I might sit at this table?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I beg your pardon.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Thank you.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, do hurry up and tell us. What have we done?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Done? Oh, it's nothing of that kind, Mrs. Ralston. It's something quite different. It's more a matter of police protection, if you understand me.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Police protection?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It relates to the death of Mrs. Lyon ― Mrs. Maureen Lyon of twenty-four Culver Street, London, West two, who was murdered yesterday, the fifteenth instant. You may have heard or read about the case?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes. I heard it on the wireless. The woman who was strangled?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's right, madam. The first thing I want to know is if you were acquainted with this Mrs. Lyon.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Never heard of her.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You mayn't have known of her under the name of Lyon. Lyon wasn't her real name. She had a police record and her fingerprints were on file, so we were able to identify her without difficulty. Her real name was Maureen Stanning. Her husband was a farmer, John Stanning, who resided at Longridge Farm not very far from here.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Longridge Farm! Wasn't that where those children...?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, the Longridge Farm case.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Three children...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's right, Miss. The Corrigans. Two boys and a girl. Brought before the court as in need of care and protection. A home was found for them with Mr. and Mrs. Stanning at Longridge Farm. One of the children subsequently died as the result of criminal neglect and persistent ill-treatment. Case made a bit of a sensation at the time.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It was horrible.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The Stannings were sentenced to terms of imprisonment. Stanning died in prison. Mrs. Stanning served her sentence and was duly released. Yesterday, as I say, she was found strangled at twenty-four Culver Street.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Who did it?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm coming to that, madam. A notebook was picked up near the scene of the crime. In that notebook was written two addresses. One was twenty-four Culver Street. The other was Monkswell Manor.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, sir. That's why Superintendent Hogben, on receiving this information from Scotland Yard, thought it imperative for me to come out here and find out if you knew of any connection between this house, or anyone in this house, and the Longridge Farm case.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: There's nothing ― absolutely nothing. It must be a coincidence.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Superintendent Hogben doesn't think it is a coincidence, sir. He'd have come himself if it had been in anyway possible. Under the weather conditions, and as I can ski, he sent me with instructions to get full particulars of everyone in the house, to report back to him by phone, and to take what measures I thought fit to ensure the safety of the household.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Safety? What danger does he think we're in? Good Lord, he's not suggesting that somebody is going to be killed here.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I don't want to frighten any of the ladies ― but frankly, yes, that is the idea.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But ― why?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's what I'm here to find out.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But the whole thing's crazy!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, sir. It's because it's crazy that it's dangerous.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Nonsense!

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I must say it seems a bit far-fetched.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I think it's wonderful.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Is there something that you haven't told us, Sergeant?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Mrs. Ralston. Below the two addresses was written "Three Blind Mice." And on the dead woman's body was a paper with "This is the First" written on it, and below the words, a drawing of three little mice and a bar of music. The music was the tune of the nursery rhyme Three Blind Mice. You know how it goes. "Three Blind Mice..."

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: "Three Blind Mice, See how they run, They all ran after the farmer's wife..." Oh, it's horrible.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: There were three children and one died?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, the youngest, a boy of eleven.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What happened to the other two?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The girl was adopted by someone. We haven't been able to trace her present whereabouts. The elder boy would now be about twenty-two. Deserted from the Army and has not been heard of since. According to the Army psychologist, was definitely schizophrenic. A bit queer in the head, that's to say.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They think that it was he who killed Mrs. Lyon ― Mrs. Stanning?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And that he's a homicidal maniac and that he will turn up here and try to kill someone ― but why?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's what I've got to find out from you. As the Superintendent sees it, there must be some connection. Now you state, sir, that you yourself have never had any connection with the Longridge Farm case?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And the same goes for you, madam?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I ― no ― I mean ― no connection.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What about servants?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: We haven't got any servants. That reminds me. Would you mind, Sergeant Trotter, if I went to the kitchen? I'll be there if you want me.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's quite all right, Mrs. Ralston. Now can I have all your names, please?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: This is quite ridiculous. We are merely staying in a kind of hotel. We only arrived yesterday. We've nothing to do with this place.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You'd planned to come here in advance, though. You'd booked your rooms here ahead.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Well, yes. All except Mr.―?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Paravicini. My car overturned in a snowdrift.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I see. What I'm getting at is that anyone who's been following you around might know very well that you were coming here. Now, there's just one thing I want to know, and I want to know it quick. Which one of you is it that has some connection with that business at Longridge Farm? You're not being very sensible, you know. One of you is in danger ― deadly danger. I've got to know which one that is. All right, I'll ask you one by one. You, first, since you seem to have arrived here more or less by accident, Mr. Pari ―?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Para ― Paravicini. But, my dear Inspector, I know nothing, but nothing, of what you have been talking about. I am a stranger in this country. I know nothing of these local affairs of bygone years.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mrs.―?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Boyle. I don't see ― really I consider it an impertinence...Why on earth should I have anything to do with such ― this distressing business?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Miss ―?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Casewell. Leslie Casewell. I never heard of Longridge Farm, and I know nothing about it.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You, sir?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Metcalf ― Major. Read about the case in the papers at the time. I was stationed at Edinburgh then. No personal knowledge.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Christopher Wren. I was a mere child at the time. I don't remember even hearing about it.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And that's all you have to say ― any of you? Well, if one of you gets murdered, you'll have yourself to blame. Now then, Mr. Ralston, can I have a look round the house?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: My dears, how melodramatic. He's very attractive, isn't he? I do admire the police. So stern and hardboiled. Quite a thrill, this whole business. Three Blind Mice. How does the tune go?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Really, Mr. Wren!

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Don't you like it? But it's a signature tune ― the signature of the murderer. Just fancy what a kick he must be getting out of it.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Melodramatic rubbish. I don't believe a word of it.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But just wait, Mrs. Boyle. Till I creep up behind you, and you feel my hands on your throat.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Stop...

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: That'll do, Christopher. It's a poor joke, anyway. In fact, it's not a joke at all.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Oh, but it is! That's just what it is. A madman's joke. That's just what makes it so deliciously macabre. If you could just see your faces!

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: A singularly ill-mannered and neurotic young man.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Where's Giles?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Taking our policeman on a conducted tour of the house.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Your friend, the architect, has been behaving in a most abnormal manner.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Young fellows seem nervy nowadays. Daresay he'll grow out of it.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Nerves? I've no patience with people who say they have nerves. I haven't any nerves.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: No? Perhaps that's just as well for you, Mrs. Boyle.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: What do you mean?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I think you were actually one of the magistrates on the Bench at the time. In fact, you were responsible for sending those three children to Longridge Farm.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Really, Major Metcalf. I can hardly be held responsible. We had reports from welfare workers. The farm people seemed very nice and were most anxious to have the children. It seemed most satisfactory. Eggs and fresh milk and a healthy out-of-doors life.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Kicks, blows, starvation, and a thoroughly vicious couple.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: But how was I to know? They were very civilly spoken.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, I was right. It was you...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: One tries to do a public duty and all one gets is abuse.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: You must forgive me, but indeed I find all this most amusing. I enjoy myself greatly.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: I never did like that man!

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Where did he come from last night?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Looks a bit of a spiv to me. Makes his face up, too. Rouge and powder. Disgusting. He must be quite old, too.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And yet he skips about as though he were quite young.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: You'll be wanting more wood. I'll get it.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's almost dark and yet it's only four in the afternoon. I'll turn the lights on. That's better.

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Now where did I leave my pen?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What a horrid little tune that is.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Don't you like it? Reminds you of your childhood, perhaps ― an unhappy childhood?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I was very happy as a child.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You were lucky.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Weren't you happy?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'm sorry.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: But all that's a long time ago. One gets over things.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I suppose so.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Or doesn't one? Damned hard to say.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They say that what happened when you're a child matters more than anything else.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: They say ― they say. Who says?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Psychologists.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: All humbug. Just a damned lot of nonsense. I've no use for psychologists and psychiatrists.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I've never really had much to do with them.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: A good thing for you you haven't. It's all a lot of hooey ― the whole thing. Life's what you make of it. Go straight ahead ― don't look back.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: One can't always help looking back.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Nonsense. It's a question of will power.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Perhaps.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I know.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I expect you're right... But sometimes things happen ― to make you remember...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Don't give in. Turn your back on them.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Is that really the right way? I wonder. Perhaps that's all wrong. Perhaps one ought really to face them.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Depends what you're talking about.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Sometimes, I hardly know what I am talking about.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Nothing from the past is going to affect me ― except in the way I want it to.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Well, everything's all right upstairs. What's in here, drawing room?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Would you mind shutting that door. This place is full of draughts.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Sorry, madam, but I've got to get the lay of the land.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie, what's all this...?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Well, that completes the tour. Nothing suspicious. I think I'll make my report now to Superintendent Hogben.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But you can't telephone. The line's dead...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What? Since when?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Major Metcalf tried it just after you arrived.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: But it was all right earlier. Superintendent Hogben got through all right.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh yes. I suppose, since then, the lines are down with the snow.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I wonder. It may have been cut.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Cut? But who could cut it?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mr. Ralston...Just how much do you know about these people who are staying in your guest house?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I ― we ― we don't really know anything about them.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Ah. {He moves above the sofa table.)

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mrs. Boyle wrote from a Bournemouth hotel, Major Metcalf from an address in ― where was it?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Leamington.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Wren wrote from Hampstead and the Casewell woman from a private hotel in Kensington. Paravicini, as we've told you, turned up out of the blue last night. Still, I suppose they've all got ration books ― that sort of thing.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I shall go into all that, of course. But there's not much reliance to be placed on that sort of evidence.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But even if this ― this maniac is trying to get here and kill us al ―-or one of us, we're quite safe now. Because of the snow. No one can get here till it melts.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Unless he's here already.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Here already?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Why not, Mr. Ralston? All these people arrived here yesterday evening. Some hours after the murder of Mrs. Stanning. Plenty of time to get here.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But except for Mr. Paravicini, they'd all booked beforehand.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Well, why not? These crimes were planned.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Crimes? There's only been one crime. In Culver Street. Why are you sure there will be another here?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That it will happen here, no ― I hope to prevent that. That it will be attempted, yes.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I can't believe it. It's so fantastic.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It isn't fantastic. It's just facts.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You've got a description of what this ― man looked like in London?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Medium height, indeterminate build, darkish overcoat, soft felt hat, face hidden by a muffler. Spoke in a whisper. There are three darkish overcoats hanging up in the hall now. One of them is yours, Mr. Ralston...There are three lightish felt hats...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I still can't believe it.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You see? It's this telephone wire that worries me. If it's been cut...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I must go and get on with the vegetables.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Is there an extension?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I beg your pardon. Did you say something?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Mr. Ralston, I said "Is there an extension?"

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Yes, up in our bedroom.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Go and try it up there for me, will you?

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Who's left this window open?

speeches.speaker: VOICE ON THE RADIO
speeches.text: ...to understand what I may term as the mechanics of fear, you have to study the precise effect produced on the human mind. Imagine, for instance, that you are alone in a room. It is late in the afternoon. A door opens softly behind you...

speeches.speaker: MRS. BOYLE
speeches.text: Oh, it's you. I can't find any programme worth listening to. Here ― what are you doing? Why did you turn out the light?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Why is it all dark? What a noise!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Now, Mrs. Ralston, try and think ― think...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I can't think. My head's numbed.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mrs. Boyle had only just been killed when you got to her. You came from the kitchen. Are you sure you didn't see or hear anybody as you came along the hallway?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No ― no, I don't think so. Just the radio blaring out in here. I couldn't think who'd turned it on so loud. I wouldn't hear anything else with that, would I?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That was clearly the murderer's idea ― or murderess.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: How could I hear anything else?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You might have done. If the murderer had left the hall that way he might have heard you coming from the kitchen. He might have slipped up the back stairs ― or into the dining room...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I think ― I'm not sure ― I heard a door creak ― and shut ― just as I came out of the kitchen.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Which door?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Think, Mrs. Ralston ― try and think. Upstairs? Downstairs? Close at hand? Right? Left?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know, I tell you. I'm not even sure I heard anything.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Can't you stop bullying her? Can't you see she's all in?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We're investigating a murder, Mr. Ralston. Up to now, nobody has taken this thing seriously. Mrs. Boyle didn't. She held out on me with information. You all held out on me. Well, Mrs. Boyle is dead. Unless we get to the bottom of this ― and quickly, mind ― there may be another death.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Another? Nonsense. Why?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Because there were three little blind mice.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: A death for each of them? But there would have to be some connection ― I mean another connection ― with the Longridge Farm business.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, there would have to be that.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But why another death here?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Because there were only two addresses in the notebook we found. Now, at twenty-four Culver Street there was only one possible victim. She's dead. But here at Monkswell Manor there is a wider field.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Nonsense. Surely it would be a most unlikely coincidence that there should be two people brought here by chance, both of them with a share in the Longridge Farm case?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Given certain circumstances, it wouldn't be so much of a coincidence. Think it out, Miss Casewell. Now I want to get down quite clearly where everyone was when Mrs. Boyle was killed. I've already got Mrs. Ralston's statement. You were in the kitchen preparing vegetables. You came out of the kitchen, along the passage, through the swing door into the hall and in here. The radio was blaring, but the light was switched off, and the hall was dark. You switched the light on, saw Mrs. Boyle, and screamed.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes. I screamed and screamed. And at last ― people came.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes. As you say, people came ― a lot of people from different directions ― all arriving more or less at once. Now then, when I got out of that window to trace the telephone wire, you, Mr. Ralston, went upstairs to the room you and Mrs. Ralston occupy, to try the extension telephone. Where were you when Mrs. Ralston screamed?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I was still up in the bedroom. The extension telephone was dead, too. I looked out of the window to see if I could see any sign of the wires being cut there, but I couldn't. Just after I closed the window again, I heard Mollie scream and I rushed down.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Those simple actions took you rather a long time, didn't they, Mr. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I don't think so.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I should say you definitely ― took your time over them.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I was thinking about something.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Very well. Now then, Mr. Wren, I'll have your account of where you were.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I'd been in the kitchen, seeing if there was anything I could do to help Mrs. Ralston. I adore cooking. After that I went upstairs to my bedroom.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Why?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: It's quite a natural thing to go to one's bedroom, don't you think? I mean ― one does want to be alone sometimes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You went to your bedroom because you wanted to be alone?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: And I wanted to brush my hair ― and ― er ― tidy up.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You wanted to brush your hair?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Anyway, that's where I was!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you heard Mrs. Ralston scream?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you came down?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Curious that you and Mr. Ralston didn't meet on the stairs.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I came down by the back stairs. They're nearer to my room.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Did you go to your room by the back stairs, or did you come through here?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I went up by the back stairs, too.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I see. Mr. Paravicini?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I have told you. I was playing the piano in the drawing room ― through there, Inspector.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm not an Inspector ― just a Sergeant, Mr. Paravicini. Did anybody hear you playing the piano?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I do not expect so. I was playing very, very softly ― with one finger ― so.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You were playing Three Blind Mice.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Is that so?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Yes. It is a very catchy little tune. It is ― how shall I say?― a haunting little tune? Don't you all agree?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I think it's horrible.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: And yet ― it runs in people's head. Someone was whistling it, too.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Whistling it? Where?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I am not sure. Perhaps in the front hall ― perhaps on the stairs ― perhaps even upstairs in a bedroom.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Who was whistling Three Blind Mice? Are you making this up, Mr. Paravicini?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: No, no, Inspector ― I beg your pardon ― Sergeant, I would not do a thing like that.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Well, go on, you were playing the piano.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: With one finger so...And then I hear the radio ― playing very loud ― someone is shouting on it. It offended my ears. And after that ― suddenly ― I hear Mrs. Ralston scream.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mr. Ralston upstairs. Mr. Wren upstairs. Mr. Paravicini in drawing room. Miss Casewell?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I was writing letters in the library.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Could you hear what was going on in here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No, I didn't hear anything until Mrs. Ralston screamed.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And what did you do then?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I came in here.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: At once.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I ― think so.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You say you were writing letters when you heard Mrs. Ralston scream?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And got up from the writing table hurriedly and came in here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And yet there doesn't seem to be any unfinished letter on the writing desk in the library.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I brought it with me.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Dearest Jessie ― h'm ― a friend of yours, or a relation?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: That's none of your damned business.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Perhaps not. You know if I were to hear someone screaming blue murder when I was writing a letter, I don't believe I'd take the time to pick up my unfinished letter, fold it and put it in my handbag before going to see what was the matter.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You wouldn't? How interesting.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Now, Major Metcalf, what about you? You say you were in the cellar. Why?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Looking around. Just looking around. I looked into that cupboard place under the stairs near the kitchen. Lot of junk and sports tackle. And I noticed there was another door inside it, and I opened it and saw a flight of steps. I was curious and I went down. Nice cellars you've got.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Glad you like them.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Not at all. Crypt of an old monastery, I should say. Probably why this place is called "Monkswell."

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We're not engaged in antiquarian research, Major Metcalf. We're investigating a murder. Mrs. Ralston has told us that she heard a door shut with a faint creak. That particular door shuts with a creak. It could be, you know, that after killing Mrs. Boyle, the murderer heard Mrs. Ralston coming from the kitchen and slipped into the cupboard pulling the door to after him.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: A lot of things could be.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: There would be fingerprints on the inside of the cupboard.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Mine are there all right. But most criminals are careful to wear gloves, aren't they?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It's usual. But all criminals slip up sooner or later.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I wonder, Sergeant, if that's really true?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Look here, aren't we wasting time? There's one person who...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Please, Mr. Ralston, I'm in charge of this investigation.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh, very well, but...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mr. Ralston! Thank you. We've got to establish opportunity, you know, as well as motive. And now let me tell you this ― you all had opportunity. There are two staircases ― anyone could go up by one and come down by the other. Anyone could go down to the cellars by the door near the kitchen and come up by a flight of steps that leads up through a trapdoor to the foot of the stairs over there. The vital fact was that every one of you was alone at the time the murder was committed.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But look here, Sergeant, you speak as though we were all under suspicion. That's absurd!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: In a murder case, everyone is under suspicion.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But you know pretty well who killed that woman in Culver Street. You think it's the eldest of those three children at the farm. A mentally abnormal young man who is now twenty-three years of age. Well, damn it all, there's only one person here who fits the bill.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: It's not true ― it's not true! You're all against me. Everyone's always been against me. You're going to frame me for a murder. It's persecution, that's what it is ― persecution.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Steady, lad, steady.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's all right, Chris. Nobody's against you. Tell him it's all right.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We don't frame people.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Tell him you're not going to arrest him.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm not arresting anyone. To do that, I've got to have evidence. I haven't got any evidence ― yet.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I think you're crazy, Mollie. And you, too! There's just one person who fits the bill and, if only as a safety measure, he ought to be put under arrest. It's only fair to the rest of us.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Wait, Giles, wait. Sergeant Trotter, can I ― can I speak to you a minute?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Certainly, Mrs. Ralston. Will the rest of you go into the dining room, please.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'm staying.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, Giles, you, too, please.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'm staying. I don't know what's come over you, Mollie.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Please.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Mrs. Ralston, what is it you want to say to me?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Sergeant Trotter, you think that this ― this crazy killer must be the ― eldest of those three boys at the Farm ― but you don't know that, do you?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We don't actually know a thing. All we've got so far is that the woman who joined with her husband in ill-treating and starving those children has been killed, and that the woman magistrate who was responsible for placing them there has been killed. The telephone wire that links me with police headquarters has been cut...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You don't even know that. It may have been just the snow.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No, Mrs. Ralston, the line was deliberately cut. It was cut just outside by the front door. I found the place.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I see.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Sit down, Mrs. Ralston.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But, all the same, you don't know...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm going by probability. It all points one way; mental instability, childish mentality, desertion from the Army and the psychiatrist's report.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, I know, and therefore it all seems to point to Christopher. But I don't believe it is Christopher. There must be other possibilities.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Such as?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well ― hadn't those children any relations at all?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The mother was a drunk. She died soon after the children were taken away from her.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What about their father?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: He was an Army sergeant, serving abroad. If he's alive, he's probably discharged from the Army by now.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You don't know where he is now?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We've no information. To trace him may take some time, but I can assure you, Mrs. Ralston, that the police take every eventuality into account.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But you don't know where he may be at this minute, and if the son is mentally unstable, the father may have been unstable, too.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Well, it's a possibility.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
