speeches.text: If he came home, after being a prisoner with the Japs, perhaps, and having suffered terribly ― if he came home and found his wife dead and that his children had gone through some terrible experience, and one of them had died through it, he might go off his head a bit and want ― revenge!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's only surmise.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But it's possible?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Oh yes, Mrs. Ralston, it's quite possible.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: So the murderer may be middle-aged, or even old. When I said the police had rung up, Major Metcalf was frightfully upset. He really was. I saw his face.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Major Metcalf?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Middle-aged. A soldier. He seems quite nice and perfectly normal ― but it mightn't show, might it?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No, often it doesn't show at all.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: So, it's not only Christopher who's a suspect. There's Major Metcalf as well.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Any other suggestions?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, Mr. Paravicini did drop the poker when I said the police had rung up.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mr. Paravicini.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I know he seems quite old ― and foreign and everything, but he mightn't really be as old as he looks. He moves like a much younger man, and he's definitely got makeup on his face. Miss Casewell noticed it, too. He might be ― oh, I know it sounds very melodramatic ― but he might be disguised.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You're very anxious, aren't you, that it shouldn't be young Mr. Wren?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He seems so ― helpless, somehow. And so unhappy.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston, let me tell you something. I've had all possibilities in mind ever since the beginning. The boy Georgie, the father ― and someone else. There was a sister, you remember.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh ― the sister?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It could have been a woman who killed Maureen Lyon. A woman. The muffler pulled up and the man's felt that pulled well down, and the killer whispered, you know. It's the voice that gives the sex away. Yes, it might have been a woman.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Miss Casewell?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: She looks a bit old for the part. Oh yes, Mrs. Ralston, there's a very wide field. There's yourself, for instance.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Me?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You're about the right age. No, no. Whatever you tell me about yourself, I've got no means of checking it at this moment, remember. And then there's your husband.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles ― how ridiculous!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: He and Christopher Wren are much of an age. Say your husband looks older than his years, and Christopher Wren looks younger. Actual age is very hard to tell. How much do you know about your husband, Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: How much do I know about Giles? Oh, don't be silly.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You've been married ― how long?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Just a year.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you met him ― where?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: At a dance in London. We went in a party.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Did you meet his people?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He hasn't any people. They're all dead.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: They're all dead?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes ― but oh, you make it sound all wrong. His father was a barrister and his mother died when he was a baby.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You're only telling me what he told you.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes ― but...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You don't know it of your own knowledge.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's outrageous that...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You'd be surprised, Mrs. Ralston, if you knew how many cases rather like yours we get. Especially since the war. Homes broken up and families dead. Fellow says he's been in the Air Force, or just finished his Army training. Parents killed ― no relations. There aren't any backgrounds nowadays and young people settle their own affairs ― they meet and marry. It's parents and relatives who used to make the enquiries before they consented to an engagement. That's all done away with. Girl just marries her man. Sometimes she doesn't find out for a year or two that he's an absconding bank clerk, or an Army deserter or something equally undesirable. How long had you known Giles Ralston when you married him?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Just three weeks. But...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you don't know anything about him?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That's not true. I know everything about him! I know exactly the sort of person he is. He's Giles. And it's absolutely absurd to suggest that he's some horrible crazy homicidal maniac. Why, he wasn't even in London yesterday when the murder took place.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Where was he? Here?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He went across country to a sale to get some wire netting for our chickens.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Bring it back with him?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, it turned out to be the wrong kind.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Only thirty miles from London, aren't you? Oh, you got an ABC? Only an hour by train ― a little longer by car.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I tell you Giles wasn't in London.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Just a minute, Mrs. Ralston. This your husband's coat?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Evening News. Yesterday's. Sold on the streets about three-thirty yesterday afternoon.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't believe it!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Don't you? Don't you?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Mollie!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, you startled me!

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Where is he? Where has he gone?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Who?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: The sergeant.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, he went out that way.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: If only I could get away. Somehow ― some way. Is there anywhere I could hide ― in the house?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Hide?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes ― from him.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Why?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But, darling, they're all so frightfully against me. They're going to say I committed these murders ― particularly your husband.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Never mind him. Listen, Christopher, you can't go on ― running away from things ― all your life.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Why do you say that?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, it's true, isn't it?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Oh yes, it's quite true.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You've got to grow up some time, Chris.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I wish I hadn't.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Your name isn't really Christopher Wren, is it?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And you're not really training to be an architect?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Why did you...?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Call myself Christopher Wren? It just amused me. And then they used to laugh at me at school and call me little Christopher Robin. Robin ― Wren ― association of ideas. It was hell being at school.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What's your real name?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: We needn't go into that. I ran away whilst I was doing my Army service. It was all so beastly ― I hated it. Yes, I'm just like the unknown murderer. I told you I was the one the specification fitted. You see, my mother my mother...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, your mother?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Everything would be all right if she hadn't died. She would have taken care of me ― and looked after me...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You can't go on being looked after all your life. Things happen to you. And you've got to bear them ― you've got to go on just as usual.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: One can't do that.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, one can.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: You mean ― you have?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What was it? Something very bad?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Something I've never forgotten.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Was it to do with Giles?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, it was long before I met Giles.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: You must have been very young. Almost a child.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Perhaps that's why it was so ― awful. It was horrible ― horrible...I try to put it out of my mind. I try never to think about it.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: So ― you're running away, too. Running away from things ― instead of facing them?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes ― perhaps, in a way, I am. Considering that I never saw you until yesterday, we seem to know each other rather well.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes, it's odd, isn't it?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know. I suppose there's a sort of ― sympathy between us.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Anyway, you think I ought to stick it out.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, frankly, what else can you do?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I might pinch the sergeant's skis. I can ski quite well.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That would be frightfully stupid. It would be almost like admitting you're guilty.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Sergeant Trotter thinks I'm guilty.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, he doesn't. At least ― I don't know what he thinks. I hate him ― I hate him ― I hate him...

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Who?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Sergeant Trotter. He puts things into your head. Things that aren't true, that can't possibly be true.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What is all this?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't believe it ― I won't believe it...

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What won't you believe? Come on ― out with it!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You see that?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What is it? Yesterday's evening paper ― a London paper. And it was in Giles's pocket. But Giles didn't go to London yesterday.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Well, if he was here all day...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: But he wasn't. He went off in the car to look for chicken wire, but he couldn't find any.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Well, that's all right. Probably he did go up to London after all.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Then why shouldn't he tell me he did? Why pretend he'd been driving all round the countryside?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Perhaps, with the news of this murder...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He didn't know about the murder. Or did he? Did he?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Good Lord, Mollie. Surely you don't think ― the Sergeant doesn't think...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know what the Sergeant thinks. And he can make you think things about people. You ask yourself questions and you begin to doubt. You feel that somebody you love and know well might be ― a stranger. That's what happens in a nightmare. You're somewhere in the middle of friends and then you suddenly look at their faces and they're not your friends any longer ― they're different people ― just pretending. Perhaps you can't trust anybody ― perhaps everybody's a stranger.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I seem to be interrupting something.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No, we were ― just talking. I must go to the kitchen ― there's the pie and potatoes ― and I must do ― do the spinach.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I'll come and give you a hand.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No, you won't.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Tête-à-têtes aren't very healthy things at present. You keep out of the kitchen and keep away from my wife.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But really, look here...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You keep away from my wife, Wren. She's not going to be the next victim.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: So that's what you think about me.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I've already said so, haven't I? There's a killer loose in this house ― and it seems to me you fit the bill.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I'm not the only one to fit the bill.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I don't see who else does.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: How blind are you ― or do you just pretend to be blind?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I tell you I'm worrying about my wife's safety.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: So am I. I'm not going to leave you here alone with her.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What the hell...?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Please go, Chris.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I'm not going.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Please go, Christopher. Please. I mean it...

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I shan't be far away.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What is all this? Mollie, you must be crazy. Perfectly prepared to shut yourself up in the kitchen with a homicidal maniac.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He isn't.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You've only got to look at him to see he's barmy.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He isn't. He's just unhappy. I tell you, Giles, he isn't dangerous. I'd know if he was dangerous. And anyway, I can look after myself.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: That's what Mrs. Boyle said!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, Giles ― don't.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Look here, what is there between you and that wretched boy?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What do you mean by between us? I'm sorry for him ― that's all.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Perhaps you'd met him before. Perhaps you suggested to him to come here and that you'd both pretend to meet for the first time. All cooked up between you, was it?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles, have you gone out of your mind? How dare you suggest these things?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Rather odd, isn't it, that he should come and stay at an out-of-the-way place like this?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: No odder than that Miss Casewell and Major Metcalf and Mrs. Boyle should.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I read once in a paper that these homicidal cases were able to attract women. Looks as though it were true. Where did you first know him? How long has this been going on?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You're being absolutely ridiculous. I never set eyes on Christopher Wren until he arrived yesterday.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: That's what you say. Perhaps you've been running up to London to meet him on the sly.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You know perfectly well that I haven't been up to London for weeks.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You haven't been up to London for weeks. Is ― that ― so?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What on earth do you mean? It's quite true.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Is it? Then what's this? This is one of the gloves you were wearing yesterday. You dropped it. I picked it up this afternoon when I was talking to Sergeant Trotter. You see what's inside it ― a London bus ticket!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh ― that...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: So it seems that you didn't only go to the village yesterday, you went to London as well.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: All right, I went to...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Whilst I was safely away racing round the countryside.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Whilst you were racing round the country-side...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Come on now ― admit it. You went to London.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: All right. I went to London. So did you!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: So did you. You brought back an evening paper.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Where did you get hold of that?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It was in your overcoat pocket.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Anyone could have put it in there.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Did they? No, you were in London.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: All right. Yes, I was in London. I didn't go to meet a woman there.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Didn't you ― are you sure you didn't?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Eh? What d'you mean?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Go away. Don't come near me.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Don't touch me.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Did you go to London yesterday to meet Christopher Wren.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Don't be a fool. Of course I didn't.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Then why did you go?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I ― shan't tell you that. Perhaps ― now ― I've forgotten why I went...

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie, what's come over you? You're different all of a sudden. I feel as though I don't know you any more.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Perhaps you never did know me. We've been married how long ― a year? But you don't really know anything about me. What I'd done or thought or felt or suffered before you knew me.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie, you're crazy...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: All right then, I'm crazy! Why not? Perhaps it's fun to be crazy!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What the hell are you...?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Now, now. I do hope you young people are not both saying a little more than you mean. One is so apt to in these lovers' quarrels.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: "Lovers' quarrels!" That's good.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Quite so. Quite so. I know just how you feel. I have been through all this myself when I was a younger man. Jeunesse ― jeunesse ― as the poet says. Not been married long, I imagine?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It's no business of yours, Mr. Paravicini...

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: No, no, no business at all. But I just came in to say that the Sergeant cannot find his skis and I'm afraid he is very annoyed.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Christopher!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What's that?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: He wants to know if you have by any chance moved them, Mr. Ralston.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No, of course not.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mr. Ralston ― Mrs. Ralston ― have you removed my skis from the cupboard back there where we put them?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Certainly not.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Somebody's taken them.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: What made you happen to look for them?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The snow is still lying. I need help here, reinforcements. I was going to ski over to the police station at Market Hampton to report on the situation.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: And now you can't ― dear, dear...Somebody's seen to it that you certainly shan't do that. But there could be another reason, couldn't there?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, what?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Somebody may want to get away.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: What did you mean when you said "Christopher" just now?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: So our young architect has hooked it, has he? Very, very interesting.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Is this true, Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, thank goodness. You haven't gone, after all.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Did you take my skis, Mr. Wren?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Your skis, Sergeant? No, why should I?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston seemed to think...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Mr. Wren is very fond of ski-ing. I thought he might have taken them just to ― get a little exercise.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Exercise?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Now, listen, you people. This is a serious matter. Somebody has removed my only chance of communication with the outside world. I want everybody here ― at once.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I think Miss Casewell has gone upstairs.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'll get her.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I left Major Metcalf in the dining room. Major Metcalf! He's not there now.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll try and find him.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Hullo, wanting me?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It's a question of my skis.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Skis?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Mr. Ralston!

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Did either of you two remove a pair of skis from the cupboard near the kitchen door?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Good Lord, no. Why should I?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: And I didn't touch 'em.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Nevertheless, they are gone. Which way did you go to your room?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: By the back stairs.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Then you passed the cupboard door.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: If you say so ― I've no idea where your skis are.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You were actually in that cupboard today.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Yes, I was.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: At the time Mrs. Boyle was killed.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: At the time Mrs. Boyle was killed I'd gone down to the cellar.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Were the skis in the cupboard when you passed through?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I haven't the least idea.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Didn't you see them there?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Can't remember.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You must remember if those skis were there then?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: No good shouting at me, young fellow. I wasn't thinking about any damned skis. I was interested in the cellars. Architecture of this place is very interesting. I opened the other door and I went on down. So I can't tell you whether the skis were there or not.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You realize that you, yourself, had an excellent opportunity of taking them?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Yes, yes, I grant you that. If I wanted to, that is.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The question is, where are they now?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Ought to be able to find them if we all set to. Not a case of "Hunt the Thimble." Whacking great things, skis. Supposing we all set to.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Not quite so fast, Major Metcalf. That maybe, you know, what we are meant to do.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Eh? I don't get you.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm in the position now where I've got to put myself in the place of a crazy cunning brain. I've got to ask myself what he wants us to do and what he, himself, is planning to do next. I've got to try and keep just one step ahead of him. Because if I don't, there's going to be another death.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You still don't believe that?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Miss Casewell. I do. Three blind mice. Two mice cancelled out ― a third mouse still to be dealt with. There are six of you here listening to me. One of you's a killer! One of you's a killer. I don't know which yet, but I shall. And another of you is the killer's prospective victim. That's the person I'm speaking to. Mrs. Boyle held out on me ― Mrs. Boyle is dead. You ― whoever you are ― are holding out on me. Well ― don't. Because you're in danger. Nobody who's killed twice is going to hesitate to kill a third time. And as it is, I don't know which of you it is who needs protection. Come on, now, anybody here who has anything, however slight, to reproach themselves for in that bygone business, had better come out with it. All right ― you won't. I'll get the killer ― I've no doubt of that ― but it may be too late for one of you. And I'll tell you another thing. The killer's enjoying this. Yes, he's enjoying himself a good deal... All right ― you can go.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Talking of chicken, dear lady, have you ever tried chickens' livers served on toast that has been thickly smeared with foie gras, with a very thin rasher of bacon just touched with a soupçon of fresh mustard? I will come with you to the kitchen and we will see what we can concoct together. A charming occupation.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'm helping my wife, Paravicini.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Your husband is afraid for you. Quite natural under the circumstances. He doesn't fancy your being alone with me. It is my sadistic tendencies he fears ― not my dishonourable ones. Alas, what an inconvenience the husband always is. Arrivederlà...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I'm sure Giles doesn't think...

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: He is very wise. Take no chances. Can I prove to you or to him or to our dogged Sergeant that I am not a homicidal maniac? So difficult to prove a negative. And suppose that instead I am really...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, don't.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: But such a gay little tune? Don't you think? She cut off their tails with a carving knife ― snick, snick, snick ― delicious. Just what a child would adore. Cruel little things, children. Some of them never grow up.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Stop frightening my wife at once.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's silly of me. But you see ― I found her. Her face was all purple. I can't forget it...

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I know. It's difficult to forget things, isn't it? You aren't really the forgetting kind.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I must go ― the food ― dinner ― prepare the spinach ― and the potatoes all going to pieces ― please, Giles.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What did you say to the lady to upset her, sir?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Me, Sergeant? Oh, just a little innocent fun. I've always been fond of a little joke.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: There's nice fun ― and there's fun that's not so nice.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Now I do wonder what you mean by that, Sergeant?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I've been doing a little wondering about you, sir.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I've been wondering about that car of yours, and how it happened to overturn in a snowdrift so conveniently.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Inconveniently, you mean, don't you, Sergeant?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That rather depends on the way you're looking at it. Just where were you bound for, by the way, when you had this ― accident?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Oh ― I was on my way to see a friend.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: In this neighbourhood?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Not so very far from here.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And what was the name and address of this friend?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Now really, Sergeant Trotter, does that matter now? I mean, it has nothing to do with this predicament, has it?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: We always like the fullest information. What did you say this friend's name was?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I didn't say.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No, you didn't say. And it seems you're not going to say. Now that's very interesting.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: But there might be ― so many reasons. An amour ― discretion. These jealous husbands.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Rather old to be running around with the ladies at your time of life, aren't you?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: My dear Sergeant, I am not, perhaps, quite so old as I look.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's just what I've been thinking, sir.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: What?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That you may not be as old as you ― try to look. There's a lot of people trying to look younger than they are. If somebody goes about trying to look older ― well, it does make one ask oneself why.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Having asked questions of so many people ― you ask questions of yourself as well? Isn't that overdoing things?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I might get an answer from myself ― I don't get many from you.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Well, well ― try again ― that is, if you have any more questions to ask.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: One or two. Where were you coming from last night?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: That is simple ― from London.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What address in London?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I always stay at the Ritz Hotel.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Very nice, too, I'm sure. What is your permanent address?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I dislike permanency.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What's your business or profession?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: I play the markets.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Stockbroker?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: No, no, you misunderstand me.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Enjoying this little game, aren't you? Sure of yourself, too. But I shouldn't be too sure. You're mixed up in a murder case, and don't you forget it. Murder isn't just fun and games.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Not even this murder? Dear me, you're very serious, Sergeant Trotter. I always have thought policemen have no sense of humour. Is the inquisition over ― for the moment?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: For the moment ― yes.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Thank you so much. I shall go and look for your skis in the drawing room. Just in case someone has hidden them in the grand piano.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Just a minute, please.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Were you speaking to me?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes. Perhaps you'd come and sit down.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Well, what do you want?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You may have heard some of the questions I was asking Mr. Paravicini?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I heard them.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'd like to have a little information from you.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: What do you want to know?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Full name, please.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Leslie Margaret Katherine Casewell.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Katherine...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I spell it with a "K."

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Quite so. Address?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Villa Mariposa, Pine d'or, Majorca.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: That's in Italy?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It's an island ― a Spanish island.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I see. And your address in England?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Care of Morgan's Bank, Leadenhall Street.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No other English address?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: How long have you been in England?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: A week.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you have been staying since your arrival...?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: At the Ledbury Hotel, Knightsbridge.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What brought you to Monkswell Manor, Miss Casewell?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I wanted somewhere quiet ― in the country.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: How long did you ― or do you ― propose to remain here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Until I've finished what I came here to do.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And what was that? And what was that?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Eh?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What was it you came here to do?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I beg your pardon. I was thinking of something else.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You haven't answered my question.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I really don't see, you know, why I should. It's a matter that concerns me alone. A strictly private affair.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: All the same, Miss Casewell...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No, I don't think we'll argue about it.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Would you mind telling me your age?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Not in the least. It's on my passport. I am twenty-four.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Twenty-four?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: You were thinking I look older. That is quite true.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Is there anyone in this country who can ― vouch for you?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: My bank will reassure you as to my financial position. I can also refer you to a solicitor ― a very discreet man. I am not in a position to offer you a social reference. I have lived most of my life abroad.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: In Majorca?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: In Majorca ― and other places.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Were you born abroad?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No, I left England when I was thirteen.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You know, Miss Casewell, I can't quite make you out.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Does it matter?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I don't know. What are you doing here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It seems to worry you.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It does worry me... You went abroad when you were thirteen?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Twelve ― thirteen ― thereabouts.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Was your name Casewell then?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It's my name now.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What was your name then? Come on ― tell me.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: What are you trying to prove?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I want to know what your name was when you left England?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It's a long time ago. I've forgotten.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: There are things one doesn't forget.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Possibly.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Unhappiness ― despair...

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I daresay...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What's your real name?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I told you ― Leslie Margaret Katherine Casewell.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Katherine...? What the hell are you doing here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I...Oh God... I wish to God I'd never come here.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: I always thought the police weren't allowed to give people the third degree.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I have merely been interrogating Miss Casewell.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: You seem to have upset her. What did he do?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: No, it's nothing. It's just ― all this ― murder ― it's so horrible. It came over me suddenly. I'll go up to my room.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It's impossible...I can't believe it...

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: What can't you believe? Six impossible things before breakfast, like the Red Queen?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Oh yes. It's rather like that.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Dear me ― you look as though you'd seen a ghost.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I've seen something I ought to have seen before. Blind as a bat, I've been. But I think now we may be able to get somewhere.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: The police have a clue.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Mr. Wren ― at last the police have a clue. I want everyone assembled in here again. Do you know where they are?

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Giles and Mollie are in the kitchen. I have been helping Major Metcalf to look for your skis. We've looked in the most entertaining places-but all to no avail. I don't know where Paravicini is.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'll get him. You get the others. Mr. Paravicini. Mr. Paravicini. Paravicini!

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Yes, Sergeant? What can I do for you? Little Bo Policeman has lost his skis and doesn't know where to find them. Leave them alone, and they'll come home, dragging a murderer behind them.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: What is all this?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Sit down, Major, Mrs. Ralston...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Must I come now? It's very inconvenient.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: There are more important things than meals, Mrs. Ralston. Mrs. Boyle, for instance, won't want another meal.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: That's a very tactless way of putting things, Sergeant.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I'm sorry, but I want co-operation and I intend to get it. Mr. Ralston, will you go and ask Miss Casewell to come down again? She went up in her room. Tell her it will only be for a few minutes.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Have your skis been found, Sergeant?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No, Mrs. Ralston, but I may say I have a very shrewd suspicion of who took them, and of why they were taken. I won't say any more at the present moment.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Please don't. I always think explanations should be kept to the very end. That exciting last chapter, you know.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: This isn't a game, sir.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: Isn't it? Now there I think you are wrong. I think it is a game ― to somebody.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: You think the murderer is enjoying himself. Maybe ― maybe.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: What is happening?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Sit down, Miss Casewell, Mrs. Ralston... Will you all pay attention, please? You may remember that after the murder of Mrs. Boyle, I took statements from you all. Those statements related to your positions at the time the murder was committed. These statements were as follows: Mrs. Ralston in the kitchen, Mr. Paravicini playing the piano in the drawing room, Mr. Ralston in his bedroom. Mr. Wren ditto. Miss Casewell in the library. Major Metcalf in the cellar.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Correct.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Those were the statements you made. I had no means of checking these statements. They may be true ― they may not. To put it quite clearly, five of those statements are true, but one is false ― which one? Five of you were speaking the truth, one of you was lying. I have a plan that may help me to discover the liar. And if I discover that one of you lied to me ― then I know who the murderer is.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Not necessarily. Someone may have lied ― for some other reason.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I rather doubt that.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: But what's the idea? You've just said you had no means of checking these statements.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: No, but supposing everyone was to go through these actions a second time.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Ah, that old chestnut. Reconstruction of the crime.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: That's a foreign idea.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Not a reconstruction of the crime, Mr. Paravicini. A reconstruction of the movements of apparently innocent persons.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: And what do you expect to learn from that?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You will forgive me if I don't make that clear just at the moment.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You want ― a repeat performance?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, Mr. Ralston, I do.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It's a trap.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: What do you mean, it's a trap?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: It is a trap. I know it is.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I only want people to do exactly what they did before.

speeches.speaker: CHRISTOPHER
speeches.text: But I don't see ― I simply can't see ― what you can possibly hope to find out by just making people do the things they did before. I think it's just nonsense.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Do you, Mr. Wren?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Well, you can count me out. I'm too busy in the kitchen.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I can't count anybody out. One might almost believe that you're all guilty by the looks of you. Why are you all so unwilling?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Of course, what you say goes, Sergeant. We'll all cooperate. Eh, Mollie?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Very well.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Wren? Miss Casewell?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Paravicini?

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Oh yes, I consent.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Metcalf?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Are we all to do exactly what we did before?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The same actions will be performed, yes.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Then I will return to the piano in the drawing room. Once again I will pick out with one finger the signature tune of a murderer. Turn, dum, dum ― dum dum dum...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Not quite so fast, Mr. Paravicini. Do you play the piano, Mrs. Ralston?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, I do.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: And you know the tune of Three Blind Mice?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Don't we all know it?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Then you could pick it out on the piano with one finger just as Mr. Paravicini did. Good. Please go into the drawing room, sit at the piano, and be ready to play when I give you the signal.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: But, Sergeant, I understood that we were each to repeat our former roles.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The same actions will be performed, but not necessarily by the same people. Thank you, Mrs. Ralston.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I don't see the point.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: There is a point. It is a means of checking up on the original statements, and maybe one statement in particular. Now then, will you all pay attention, please. I will assign each of you your new stations. Mr. Wren, will you kindly go to the kitchen. Just keep an eye on Mrs. Ralston's dinner for her. You're very fond of cooking, I believe. Mr. Paravicini, will you go up to Mr. Wren's room. By the back stairs is the most convenient way. Major Metcalf, will you go up to Mr. Ralston's room and examine the telephone there. Miss Casewell, would you mind going down to the cellars? Mr. Wren will show you the way. Unfortunately, I need someone to reproduce my own actions. I am sorry to ask it of you, Mr. Ralston, but would you go out by that window and follow the telephone wire round to near the front door. Rather a chilly job ― but you're probably the toughest person here.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: And what are you going to do?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I am enacting the part of Mrs. Boyle.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Taking a bit of a risk, aren't you?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You will all stay in your places and remain there until you hear me call you.

speeches.speaker: PARAVICINI
speeches.text: Parlour games!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No objection to my wearing a coat?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I should advise it, sir. Take my torch, sir. It's behind the curtain. Mrs. Ralston, count twenty and then begin to play. Mrs. Ralston! Mrs. Ralston!

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes, what is it? You're looking very pleased with yourself. Have you got what you wanted?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: I've got exactly what I wanted.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You know who the murderer is?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, I know.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Which of them?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You ought to know, Mrs. Ralston.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, you've been extraordinary foolish, you know. You've run a very good chance of being killed by holding out on me. As a result, you've been in serious danger more than once.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't know what you mean.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Come now, Mrs. Ralston. We policemen aren't quite so dumb as you think. All along I've realized that you had firsthand knowledge of the Longridge Farm affair. You knew Mrs. Boyle was the magistrate concerned. In fact, you knew all about it. Why didn't you speak up and say so?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I don't understand. I wanted to forget ― forget.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Your maiden name was Waring?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Miss Waring. You taught school ― in the school where those children went.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Yes.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It's true, isn't it, that Jimmy, the child who died, managed to get a letter posted to you? The letter begged for help ― help from his kind young teacher. You never answered that letter.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I couldn't. I never got it.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You just ― didn't bother.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That's not true. I was ill. I went down with pneumonia that very day. The letter was put aside with others. It was weeks afterwards that I found it with a lot of other letters. And by then that poor child was dead... Dead ― dead...Waiting for me to do something ― hoping ― gradually losing hope...Oh, it's haunted me ever since...If only I hadn't been ill ― if only I'd known...Oh, it's monstrous that such things should happen.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Yes, it's monstrous.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I thought the police didn't carry revolvers...

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: The police don't... I'm not a policeman, Mrs. Ralston. You thought I was a policeman because I rang up from a call box and said I was speaking from police headquarters and that Sergeant Trotter was on his way. I cut the telephone wires before I came to the front door. You know who I am, Mrs. Ralston? I'm Georgie ― I'm Jimmy's brother, Georgie.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: You'd better not scream, Mrs. Ralston ― because if you do I shall fire this revolver...I'd like to talk to you a little. I said I'd like to talk to you a little. Jimmy died. That nasty cruel woman killed him. They put her in prison. Prison wasn't bad enough for her. I said I'd kill her one day...I did, too. In the fog. It was great fun. I hope Jimmy knows. "I'll kill them all when I've grown up." That's what I said to myself. Because grown-ups can do anything they like. I'm going to kill you in a minute.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You'd better not. You'll never get safely away, you know.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Someone's hidden my skis! I can't find them. But it doesn't matter. I don't really mind if I get away or not. I'm tired. It's all been such fun. Watching you all. And pretending to be a policeman.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: That revolver will make a lot of noise.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: It will rather. Much better to do it the usual way, and take you by the neck. The last little mouse in the trap.

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Georgie, Georgie, you know me, don't you? Don't you remember the farm, Georgie? The animals, that fat old pig, and the day the bull chased us across the field. And the dogs.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Dogs?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Yes, Spot and Plain.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Kathy?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: Yes, Kathy ― you remember me now, don't you?

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Kathy, it is you. What are you doing here?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: I came to England to find you. I didn't recognize you until you twirled your hair the way you always used to do. Yes, you always did it. Georgie, come with me. You're coming with me.

speeches.speaker: TROTTER
speeches.text: Where are we going?

speeches.speaker: MISS CASEWELL
speeches.text: It's all right, Georgie. I'm taking you somewhere where they will look after you, and see that you won't do any more harm.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Ralston! Ralston!

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Mollie, Mollie, are you all right? Darling, darling.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, Giles.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Whoever would have dreamt it was Trotter?

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: He's mad, quite mad.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Yes, but you...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I was mixed up in it all, I taught in the school. It wasn't my fault ― but he thought I could have saved that child.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: You should have told me.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: I wanted to forget.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Everything's under control. He will be unconscious soon with a sedative ― his sister's looking after him. Poor fellow's as mad as a hatter, of course. I've had my suspicions of him all along.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You did? Didn't you believe he was a policeman?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: I knew he wasn't a policeman. You see, Mrs. Ralston, I'm a policeman.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: As soon as we got hold of that notebook with "Monkswell Manor" written in it, we saw it was vital to have someone on the spot. When it was put to him, Major Metcalf agreed to let me take his place. I couldn't understand it when Trotter turned up.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And Casewell is his sister?

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Yes, it seems she recognized him just before this last business. Didn't know what to do, but fortunately came to me about it, just in time. Well, it's started to thaw, help should be here pretty soon. Oh, by the way, Mrs. Ralston, I'll remove those skis. I hid them on top of the fourposter.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: And I thought it was Paravicini.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I gather they'll examine that car of his rather carefully. I shouldn't be surprised if they found a thousand or so Swiss watches in the spare wheel. Yes, that's his line of business, nasty little bit of goods. Mollie, I believe you thought I was...

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Giles, what were you doing in London yesterday?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Darling, I was buying you an anniversary present. We've been married just a year today.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh. That's what I went to London for, and I didn't want you to know.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: No.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: They're cigars. I do hope they're all right.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh, darling, how sweet of you. They're splendid.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: You will smoke them?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: I'll smoke them.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: What's my present?

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Oh yes, I forgot all about your present. It's a hat.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: A hat? But I practically never wear one.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Just for best.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, how lovely, darling.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: Put it on.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Later, when my hair's done properly.

speeches.speaker: GILES
speeches.text: It is all right, isn't it? The girl in the shop said it was the last thing in hats.

speeches.speaker: MAJOR METCALF
speeches.text: Mrs. Ralston! Mrs. Ralston! There's a terrible smell of burning coming from the kitchen.

speeches.speaker: MOLLIE
speeches.text: Oh, my pie!
